turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on through, both of you. What would you like to sort out today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the repeats, but honestly I'm more bothered about this knee. I need something stronger. These tablets aren't doing a thing.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's been saying that since Monday. I thought we'd do the whole list while the pharmacy technician's still got his bag downstairs.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. Start wherever you like, what's the knee actually doing?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Right knee. Deep ache, and then a stab if I twist. Um, going round the shops sets it off something awful.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long's it been like that?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Six months. Well, actually, I was going to say since autumn, but six months sounds right. I think.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Longer. He was limping at Christmas, so it's over a year. He just forgets.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't forget. I... Christmas is a blur. I'm saying six months.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): So we'll call it roughly six months to a year, and not pretend we've dated it. Is it there every day?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Most days. Mornings it's stiff, then it eases if I potter. Walking makes the ache worse. If I sit with the leg up it eases off a bit.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it swell, or give way under you?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Puffs up by the evening. Hasn't given way. I haven't fallen, touch wood.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the rest of you, chest pain, shortness of breath, trouble with the waterworks?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain, breathing's alright, waterworks are fine. I'm just sick of the knee.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sleep's a mess, though. He's up in the night with it.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): The knee wakes me, yes. I'm not depressed, if that's what you're thinking. I just can't get comfy.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wasn't thinking that. Before the tablets, did you get here alright? I was stuck on the bypass for ages.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Forty minutes, easy. A lorry had tipped pallets all over the retail park. Ridiculous.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Then this car park was full, so round the block we went. He had the cricket on the whole time.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): England were hopeless. My grandson Alfie had the radio on at breakfast, seven years old and shouting at the bowlers. I nearly switched it off.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And he made me pull in at the bakery. Cinnamon bun, icing on his jumper, doctor's waiting room. Honestly.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Worth it. Have you seen that sky? It's going to bucket down, my neighbour said. Her hanging baskets are already sulking.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): I left a sheet out on the line, so that'll be that. Shall we come back to the medicines? What are you taking just now?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The pain ones, co-codamol. My water tablet. The sugar tablets for the diabetes. And the little white one for the cholesterol, atorvastatin, that's the name.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Take me through the co-codamol. What strength do you reckon, and how do you take it?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): The strong ones. Thirty with five hundred. Two tablets, four times a day. That's what goes down.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's not what this says. The pharmacy technician printed the list off the bag. Co-codamol eight slash five hundred, two tablets up to four times a day.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Eight? That can't be mine. Are you reading the wrong line? The box looks exactly the same as last time.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then what you believe and what the list says don't match, and I'm not going to invent a strength. The two tablets, four times a day, you both happy with that bit?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Two, four times. I don't skip them. Why would the list be wrong? Could the technician have typed it wrong?
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Possibly. We'll let the chemist confirm it. Now, the water tablet, do you know what it actually is?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Bendro-thingy. Bendroflumethiazide. Two and a half milligrams, mornings. It's for the blood pressure. Makes me trot to the loo, mind.
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He does take that every morning. I see him.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the sugar tablets, which ones, and how much?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Metformin. Five hundred milligrams twice a day, with my meals. Years I've been on those.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Atorvastatin next. What dose is on the packet?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty milligrams at night. I think. Or forty? No, hang on, the packet says twenty. I'm fairly sure. Fairly.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's twenty. I looked on Sunday.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything you've come off, or a box you were given and never started?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Naproxen. I stopped that in March, it burned my stomach. And gabapentin, they handed me a box and I never took a single one. Still sitting there.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gabapentin we simply ignore, then. Naproxen stays off. You said you wanted something stronger, what were you hoping for?

[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Tramadol. My neighbour gets it and she says it's marvellous. Or morphine, if that's what bad knees get. Why won't people just give it? Will it clash with the sugar tablets? What if I wake at three and I've already had four lots of co-codamol?

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not starting tramadol, and I'm not starting morphine. Let me think it through out loud. This could be the osteoarthritis grumbling, it could be extra time on your feet, it could be pain referred from the hip. I am not concluding any of those, and I am not calling it a nerve problem or a clot. Not from this chat.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're saying you don't know? That's worse. What am I meant to do tonight?
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I do have a working impression. It's your known osteoarthritis flaring in that right knee. That's the leading thought, and I'm stopping there.

[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Then a stronger tablet is obvious, isn't it? What about plain codeine? Or one of those gels? Is the gel useless? Will it count as another anti-inflammatory and burn me again?

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Plain codeine on top of co-codamol just stacks the codeine, so no. No tramadol either. A gel is different. I'll add ibuprofen gel, three times a day, rubbed on the knee. It's not the same as swallowing naproxen.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): And my stomach will be alright? I have a whisky on a Sunday, is that banned now? What about paracetamol from the corner shop as well?
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gel on the skin is much kinder on the stomach; stop if the skin goes sore. Sunday whisky is fine. Don't add shop painkillers on top of the co-codamol.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): One whisky, that's his lot. And he doesn't smoke, never has.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): May I have a look at the knee while you're here?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): If you must. It'll hurt, I'm warning you.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right knee's a little puffy, not red, and you flex to about ninety before you pull away. The hip moves freely, so that referral idea can sit down.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): See, it hurts. Are you sending me for an x-ray? What if it's cracked? Should I be on a stick?

[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): No x-ray today. If it hasn't settled by the time I see you again, we might do a plain film, but I'm not booking it now. A stick only if you feel safer, not because I think it's broken.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): And you won't cancel the sugar tablets or the water one, will you? What if they send the weak co-codamol and it's not enough? Can I take an extra two?

[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll re-authorise the metformin, the bendroflumethiazide and the atorvastatin exactly as they are. Co-codamol stays, but I will not increase it, and the chemist confirms eight or thirty before the next issue. No extra tablets. I'll add the ibuprofen gel to the repeat.
[SEG0059] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll phone the chemist after this and make them read the bag back to me.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Come back and see me in six weeks either way. Sooner if the knee blows up, you can't walk on it, or it goes hot and red.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks is ages. What if the gel runs out? Should I keep pottering in the garden or will I ruin it? And ice, is ice daft?

[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep pottering, little and often, leg up when it throbs, ice in a tea towel for ten minutes if it's puffy. The gel's on the repeat so it shouldn't run out. Any allergies before I send the script?
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I've had penicillin, no rash, no trouble. I'm not allergic to anything.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then we're done. Go careful if that rain starts.

spec.situation: Routine repeat-prescription review at a small clinic with a pharmacy technician present; patient wants a stronger painkiller; tablet names and doses are discussed in detail, one dose is read from the pharmacy list and differs from the patient's own; doctor declines the stronger medicine.
features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

bad.reason: Continue co-codamol and no increase supported; 'only after' chemist confirmation is not stated.
bad.text: Continue co-codamol without increasing the strength, only after the chemist confirms 8/500 or 30/500 (action_type=medication, status=conditional, responsible_person=doctor)

omissions.text: Right knee pain is a deep ache with a stabbing pain on twisting; walking makes the ache worse and resting with the leg elevated eases it somewhat; present on most days.
Gabapentin was prescribed/given previously but the patient never started it and still has the box at home; doctor said to ignore it.

Patient denied the knee being hot/red currently; these were given as return precautions, but current absence was implied by exam only. More importantly, allergy history included tolerance of penicillin: 'I've had penicillin, no rash, no trouble.'
Doctor explicitly decided not to start tramadol or morphine and also not to add plain codeine because it would duplicate codeine with co-codamol.
Doctor said no x-ray today and not booking it now; only consider a plain film later if not settled by next review.

Doctor stated differential considerations that were specifically not concluded from the chat: could be osteoarthritis, extra time on feet, or referred pain from the hip; not concluding nerve problem or clot.
